Okay, so I need to figure out which action explains how a somatic cell mutation can harm an organism. The options are A) creating a dominant allele, B) affecting gamete formation, C) leading to tumors in tissue, and D) being passed on to offspring.

First, I remember that somatic cell mutations occur in the body cells, not the reproductive cells. So, they don't get passed on to offspring, which means D is probably not the right answer. That leaves A, B, and C.

Option A talks about creating a dominant allele. I think dominant alleles are related to genetic traits, but a somatic mutation isn't about creating a new allele. It's more about changes in existing cells, so maybe A isn't the right choice.

Option B is about affecting gamete formation. Gametes are the reproductive cells, but somatic mutations happen in body cells, not the germ cells. So B might not be correct either.

That leaves C, leading to tumors in tissue. I recall that mutations in somatic cells can cause cells to grow uncontrollably, leading to tumors. That makes sense because cancer is a common result of such mutations. So C seems like the correct answer.

Wait, but the initial answer given was D. Did I miss something? Let me double-check. Somatic mutations don't affect gametes or offspring, so D is incorrect. A is about alleles, which isn't directly related to harm from mutations. So yes, C is the right choice.
</think>
